This modest decline during incubation likely reflects the metabolic consumption of albumen and yolk reserves by the developing embryo. Following hatching, the downy chick depends entirely on its parents for thermoregulation and regurgitated food, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult reaches 687 grams [Wwi = 687 grams], an asymptotic mass that places this species near the middle of the size range for the Laridae family. This adult body mass is attained after a predictable developmental schedule that is tightly linked to the thermal conditions experienced during early life.

This period of embryonic development is notably longer than that of many smaller Laridae, which typically hatch in under 25 days, a difference that may correlate with the relatively large yolk volume of the Swallow-tailed gull egg. The considerable energy reserves contained within the egg at laying allow the embryo to sustain itself through this extended incubation without requiring external feeding, highlighting an adaptive strategy for a species that nests on remote cliff ledges where parental attentiveness during incubation may be intermittent.

The species exhibits an exceptionally low maximum reproductive rate, laying a single egg per clutch and producing only a single clutch each year, resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. This unusually high efficiency reflects minimal water loss through the porous calcareous shell during incubation, an adaptation that ensures the neonate begins life with robust energy reserves.
